letter.subject: Concern regarding cookie and tracking activity after rejection of optional cookies on pearson.com
letter.body:
Dear Data Protection Officer,

I am writing to raise concerns identified during an automated, passive audit of https://pearson.com on 2026-11-08 04:13 UTC. Using a fresh browser, the audit detected the cookie banner, clicked the “Reject All” option, then browsed pages on your site and recorded what was still sent afterwards.

The pages visited after rejection were:
1. https://www.pearson.com/en-gb/schools.html
2. https://www.pearson.com/en-us
3. https://www.pearson.com/en-ca.html

The privacy notice reviewed was:
1. https://www.pearson.com/en-ca/privacy-center/privacy-notices.html

Our concerns are as follows:
1. Our automated review suggests tracking cookies were set after consent was rejected. After the banner’s “Reject All” option was clicked, new Google cookies with apparent unique identifiers were set on .youtube.com. This appears to conflict with the statement in your policy that “Optional cookies will only be set with your consent.”
2. We observed that Google still received data after cookies were rejected. After rejection, 67 requests were made to google-analytics.com, googlesyndication.com, googletagmanager.com and youtube.com. We also observed new cookies being set after rejection: VISITOR_INFO1_LIVE, VISITOR_PRIVACY_METADATA, YSC, __Secure-ROLLOUT_TOKEN and __Secure-YNID.
3. We observed that Microsoft still received data after cookies were rejected, including 1 request to bing.com.
4. We observed that three tracking companies were not named in the privacy notice reviewed. The policy names 0 companies, and we found no mention of Google, Microsoft or New Relic. We recognise the policy may refer to recipients only by category.

Please would you:
1. Explain each of the points above.
2. Confirm which cookies, trackers and related requests you consider strictly necessary or otherwise exempt from consent, and why.
3. Stop any non-essential cookies or tracking technologies from being set or used before consent is obtained.
4. Reply within one month.

If this matter is not resolved, it may be raised with the Information Commissioner’s Office.

Yours faithfully,
Joshua Baker
